name: Redensyl

lead: Redensyl is a cosmetic ingredient in over-the-counter hair serums and lotions. People apply it to thinning areas hoping for thicker-looking hair and a denser hairline, either on its own or alongside drug treatments.

Its maker says it reactivates dormant follicle stem cells, a claim supported by lab and ex vivo work. Published human studies are small, test finished products that blend Redensyl with other actives, and often have industry-linked authors.

paras: It is used as a leave-on scalp serum or lotion, applied to thinning areas as part of a regular routine. Many people layer it with other topical or prescription hair-loss treatments. Users generally describe results as gradual, over several months of consistent use.

The small studies reported no significant adverse events. It is regulated as a cosmetic, not an approved hair-loss drug. Because it is plant-derived, people sensitive to plant extracts are advised to patch-test first.

angle.text: Users apply Redensyl serums to thinning areas hoping for fuller hair and a denser-looking hairline. It is used as a cosmetic alternative or add-on to drug treatments, working through claimed stimulation of follicle stem cells. Human studies so far are small, industry-linked tests of multi-ingredient products.

lead: Redensyl is a patented cosmetic active ingredient for anti-hair-loss serums and lotions, developed by Givaudan Active Beauty (formerly Induchem). According to Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, it combines a larch-derived dihydroquercetin glucoside, a green tea derivative (EGCG2), glycine and zinc chloride, and is used at roughly 1 to 3 percent. [1]

The manufacturer-style claim is that it reactivates dormant hair follicle stem cells; the supporting data described in that source are in vitro or ex vivo. [1] Published human studies are small and typically test finished products that contain Redensyl together with other actives, often with industry-linked authors. [2][3][4]
Redensyl is regulated as a cosmetic ingredient rather than a drug, so products carrying it are not approved to treat hair loss. [1]
infobox: Dihydroquercetin glucoside, EGCG2, glycine, zinc chloride [1]
Cosmetic ingredient, not an approved drug [1]

paras: Redensyl is sold to cosmetic manufacturers as a proprietary blend rather than a single molecule. Grokipedia describes the main active as dihydroquercetin glucoside, with the exact ratios proprietary. [1]

The claimed mechanism is stimulation of hair follicle stem cells and outer root sheath cells, with increased proliferation markers and Wnt pathway activity. The same source says these results come from cell culture and ex vivo follicle experiments and have not been directly shown to apply in living scalps. [1]

A 2020 randomized, single-blinded, vehicle-controlled study randomized 44 people with androgenetic alopecia to a lotion containing Redensyl and Sepicontrol A5 or a vehicle, twice daily for 24 weeks. Its authors reported improvements in investigator-assessed outcomes and the anagen-to-telogen ratio in the active group, with no significant adverse events. [2] The tested product combined two actives, so effects cannot be assigned to Redensyl alone.

A 2024 study of 32 adults used a serum containing Redensyl, AnaGain, Procapil and other ingredients daily for 60 days; the authors reported increased hair growth rate and no adverse events. [3] A 2025 open-label, single-arm study of a rosemary and Redensyl serum in women over 120 days reported improvements across several measures, with no adverse effects. [5] The latter two studies had no control group in the abstracts described and were conducted by authors affiliated with a contract research firm and, in one case, the product company.

A 2023 randomized trial of 54 men compared platelet-rich plasma plus topical Procapil with platelet-rich plasma plus a Redensyl, saw palmetto and biotin product; the AGA grade differed significantly between groups in favour of the Redensyl combination. [4] A 2025 review of topical hair products discusses Redensyl among 'hyped' ingredients and weighs the clinical evidence available. [6]

Studies above report no significant adverse events, although they were short and small. [2][3][5] Grokipedia says Redensyl is regulated as a cosmetic ingredient in the EU and US, so labels cannot make medical claims, and that people with plant allergies are advised to patch-test. [1]
